competitors.name: TeamSnap
competitors.model: Freemium. Free basic tier; paid team plans ~$10-20/mo per team (last price rise Mar 1 2023, first since 2018). Notably sells ad removal as a separate IAP: App Store lists "TeamSnap Ad Free" at $2.49 and $5.99, and "TeamSnap+ Content & Ad-Free" at $6.99/$7.99/$49.99/$59.99.
competitors.note: The incumbent, 4.8 stars on 59K iOS ratings, claims 25M users. Owns rosters, schedule, availability/RSVP, chat, payments. Weak spots: RSVP/availability is gated off the free tier so Free behaves as an extended trial; ads are shown to free users AND sold back as an upsell; Capterra reviewers repeatedly cite sync failures and support that replies in 1-5 days with links.

competitors.name: SignUpGenius
competitors.model: Free with ads; paid tiers remove ads (exact tier prices NOT verified, a third-party roundup puts comparable tools at ~$9/mo).
competitors.note: The actual default for the snack-schedule job specifically, not TeamSnap. Unlimited participants free, reminders, templates. The fatal detail, confirmed on SignUpGenius's own help page: ads render on the participant signup page too, not just the organizer dashboard, 'people signing up through free account sign-ups may see ads.' Capterra reviewers also call the design dated and flag that deleted users can still reach signups via old email links.

competitors.name: GameChanger (DICK'S / Stack Sports)
competitors.model: Free for team messaging, scheduling and RSVP; monetized on streaming/video/AI film subscriptions. MLB and GoPro partnerships.
competitors.note: 9M+ active users, 1M+ teams, ~9M games/yr, effectively the default in baseball and softball, expanding into basketball/volleyball. Coordination is free because scorekeeping and video is the paid product. Strong where a team already scores games in it; irrelevant for sports it does not cover, and it does not do snack duty.

competitors.name: TeamReach
competitors.model: Free. Join by team code, 'no phone numbers or emails exchanged.'
competitors.note: Closest philosophical competitor to our stance and proof the no-account model works at scale (4.6 stars, 7K iOS ratings). But it is still a native download, and reviews show classic native failure modes: 'any time you leave the app to do things like check your availability, the app resets'; notifications 'does not always come through'; a recent update broke calendar sync and stability; posts sort by most-recently-commented so people miss them. One reviewer notes the code model has no gate at all: 'all I needed was a name.'

competitors.name: Spond
competitors.model: Free core product; monetized via payments/fundraising.
competitors.note: Large in Europe, growing in the US. Publishes actively on youth data privacy, which shows privacy is a live differentiator buyers respond to. Rounded, friendly, modern UI, the visual benchmark to beat, not TeamSnap.

competitors.name: Heja
competitors.note: Swedish, founded 2018, still actively shipping as of mid-2026 (App Store and Google Play updates through June 2026). Deliberately simple: schedule, availability, chat, reminders. Marketed as 'all you need to run a youth sports team, free.' The simplicity competitor.

competitors.name: The group text + a Google Sheet + a printed snack sheet on the fridge
competitors.note: THIS is the real competitor and it is winning. Documented failure modes: parents overwrite each other's cells, terrible on mobile, no reminders, no slot limits; and the text thread degenerates, the canonical description is 'the carpool fell apart in a group text with 47 unread messages.' Paper 'gets rained on, crumpled in gym bags, and forgotten at home.' We must beat this on setup time and on the recipient's four-second glance, not on feature count.

competitors.name: Skylight Calendar 2
competitors.model: Hardware: $299.99 (15") / $599.99 (27" Max) plus Skylight Plus at $79/yr.
competitors.note: Not a direct competitor but a market tell: families will spend $300-600 plus a subscription purely to answer 'who has to be where.' Harris Poll 2024 via Youth Sports Business Report: parents spend 30.4 hrs/wk on family logistics, ~17.5 weekly comms about kids' schedules, kids average 11.5 activities/wk. The pain is worth real money, a free tool that nails the glance is valuable, not a toy.

complaints.complaint: "I sent the [signup] link and several parents said they thought it was spam because of all the ads." Ads render on the participant-facing signup page, so the team parent's carefully shared link arrives looking like a content farm, and some parents refuse to click it.
complaints.source: Quoted in SignUpReady's 2026 snack-schedule roundup; underlying ad behavior confirmed on SignUpGenius's own help page ('people signing up through free account sign-ups may see ads')
complaints.weWinIf: The shared link opens on a clean, ad-free, interstitial-free page that looks like a person made it. Put a literal one-line trust stamp near the top of the shared view, 'No ads. No account. Nothing tracked.', because the recipient's first reflex is 'is this spam?' and answering it costs us one sentence. No cookie banner, no email gate, no 'open in app' bounce.

complaints.complaint: "The amount of ads in the app and on the website is beyond nauseating unless you want to pay another $2 a month." TeamSnap literally ships IAPs named 'TeamSnap Ad Free' at $2.49 and $5.99, ad removal is a product SKU on top of the team subscription.
complaints.source: Capterra TeamSnap reviews; IAP names and prices read off the App Store listing (id393048976)
complaints.weWinIf: Ad-free is the product, not a $2.49 upsell. Never show a paywall, a 'go premium' badge, a locked feature, or a greyed-out button. The tip jar is one quiet link in an About/footer position, never a modal, and never on the shared parent view.

complaints.complaint: "Setting up your roster and getting the parents onto the app was the hardest part" / "it was hard to get team engagement or buy-in for the app." The organizer does the work and then has to nag 14 families to install something and make an account.
complaints.weWinIf: There is no adoption step. A parent who taps the link is already fully onboarded, the season is on screen in under a second, no install, no code, no name entry. Make this the headline claim: 'They don't have to download anything.' This is our biggest structural advantage and should be the first thing the organizer reads.

complaints.complaint: Notifications silently fail across the whole category. TeamSnap: "Our team is getting notifications approximately 30% of the time when someone sends a chat message." TeamReach: "notifications does not always come through. Messages sent to the group may not reach everyone."
complaints.source: App Store reviews for TeamSnap (id393048976) and TeamReach (id1101253705)
complaints.weWinIf: Do not compete on push, we can't, and neither can they, reliably. Invert it: give the organizer a one-tap 'copy this week' block formatted for SMS ('Sat 9/12 vs Hawks · Field 4 · arrive 8:30 · blue jerseys · Snacks: the Ramirez family'), so the message goes out over the channel parents actually read. Being honest that the link is the source of truth and text is the nudge beats a broken bell icon.

complaints.complaint: "Any time you leave the app to do things like check your availability, the app resets", you get bounced to the top and have to re-navigate to where you were.
complaints.weWinIf: All state survives reload, backgrounding, and a killed tab. Deep-link to a specific game so 'here's Saturday' opens on Saturday. Any checkbox or claimed slot persists instantly with no save button.

complaints.complaint: Google Sheets as the snack schedule: "parents overwrite cells, poor mobile experience, no reminders, no slot limits." One fat-thumb edit silently wipes another family's slot and nobody notices until the week it matters.
complaints.weWinIf: Claiming a slot is a tap on a thumb-sized row, and a taken slot cannot be silently overwritten, it shows who has it. Swaps are explicit ('trade with the Chens'), not destructive edits. Mobile-first layout, never a horizontally scrolling table.

complaints.complaint: Rosters expose kids badly: "Team rosters included full names, full date of birth, and e-mail address of the parent, all in one place and available online for anyone who took the time to look." Youth sports orgs collect addresses, photos and birthdays and are documented as poor at protecting them.
complaints.source: Christian Science Monitor, 'When it comes to privacy, youth sports strike out'; National Sports ID data-privacy writeups; Spond's own youth-data-privacy blog
complaints.weWinIf: Data lives on the organizer's device by default. On the shared view, kids default to first name + last initial and parent phone numbers are opt-in per family, with a visible toggle the organizer controls. Turn the constraint into something the organizer can point to when a nervous parent asks. Never put a child's birthdate in the product at all.

complaints.complaint: "You'll never talk to a live person and they don't care...They're awful", support replies in 1-5 days, "not with a call but usually with links." Separately, a 2024 reviewer locked out of their account: "We've spent six days, 2-3 hours a day, trying to fix the issue with no help."
complaints.source: Capterra and App Store reviews, TeamSnap
complaints.weWinIf: There is no account to be locked out of, so the account-recovery failure mode cannot exist. Back it up with an always-available escape hatch: export the season as a printable sheet and as a plain-text block, so nobody is ever trapped or waiting on us.

complaints.complaint: Calendar import is a known dead end: "There were advertisements and I'm not sure how to import the schedule into my calendar." TeamReach users separately complain the app demands 'allow full access' to their calendar instead of write-only.
complaints.source: Capterra TeamSnap review; App Store TeamReach reviews
complaints.weWinIf: One button: download the whole season as a .ics the parent double-taps into Apple/Google Calendar. No permission prompt, no OAuth, no access to their calendar at all, we hand them a file. Put the field name and address in the event LOCATION so the calendar entry itself is navigable.

complaints.complaint: The tools are rigid mid-season, "Once a group chat is created, you cannot add a member to the group", while schedules change constantly: "Practice moved to Tuesday. The tournament bracket dropped at 9 p.m."
complaints.source: Capterra TeamSnap review; Youth Sports Business Report / Good Game newsletter
complaints.weWinIf: Every edit is live on the same link, the organizer never re-shares. Add a mid-season player, move a game, or cancel for rain in under 15 seconds, and surface a dated 'Updated Tue 6:10pm, Sat game moved to Field 2' banner at the top of the shared view so parents can trust what they're seeing is current.

complaints.complaint: Cost stacking on top of an already expensive hobby, paid by a volunteer. TeamSnap runs ~$10-20/mo/team on top of registration, uniforms and travel, and the person paying is usually the team parent out of pocket. Roughly 61% of sports parents volunteer, adding ~4.2 hrs/week of unpaid labor.
complaints.source: TeamSnap pricing pages / Capterra; volunteer-load figures from youth-sports coverage of team-manager burnout
complaints.weWinIf: $0, permanently, with no card and no trial clock. Say the quiet part out loud in the marketing: 'You already volunteered your Saturdays. You shouldn't also be expensing a subscription.'

complaints.complaint: "The design looks dated compared to other platforms," and "there is a bit of a learning curve... the features and directions are not very clearly described."
complaints.weWinIf: A modern, typographically confident page is a cheap and immediately visible win against the category's default incumbent. The organizer flow must be walk-up-usable in one screen: paste or type the game dates, pick a roster, done, no wizard, no eight-step setup, no glossary of 'events vs. activities.'

tableStakes: One shareable link (plus a QR) covering the whole season that opens read-only for parents with zero install and zero account. If a parent has to type a code or a name, we have already lost the comparison to a text message.

Auto-generated snack/duty rotation across the real game dates, fair round-robin from the roster in one tap, with manual override, a 'we're away that weekend' skip, and explicit swaps. Building the rotation slot-by-slot is the chore every competitor still makes you do.

Game entries carrying date, start time, arrive-by time, opponent, field NAME, and a tappable address that opens Maps, plus uniform/jersey color. 'Which field?' and 'what color shirt?' are the two texts the team parent gets every Saturday morning.

A 'Next up' answer block pinned to the top of the shared view, this week's game and whose snack turn it is, in large type, above any table. Parents give this four seconds in a parking lot; a full-season grid as the landing state reads as amateur.

Roster with per-family contact and tap-to-call / tap-to-text links, plus a team-wide allergy and dietary-restriction note. Allergies are the first thing every snack-schedule guide tells organizers to collect, and their absence is a safety-flavored failure.
Check-off and claim state that survives reload, tab kill, and backgrounding, no save button, no lost place.
Season .ics export for calendar import with LOCATION populated. Every roundup and review surfaces manual calendar entry as a top annoyance.
A printable, fridge-worthy one-page season sheet with the snack rotation and the QR code on it. Paper is the format that survives a dead phone, and the QR turns the paper back into the live version.

Copy-as-text output the organizer can paste straight into the existing group chat, for the season and for a single week. Meeting parents in the channel they already read is table stakes now, not a nicety.
Full offline function with a visible 'showing your saved copy' state. Youth fields have no signal; a spinner at 8:15am on a Saturday is a broken app.
differentiators: One-tap 'copy this week' SMS block. Routes around the notification unreliability every competitor suffers from, by handing the organizer a perfectly formatted text instead of a bell icon that fires 30% of the time.

Auto-fair snack rotation generated from roster + schedule in a single tap, with blackout dates per family. Everyone else makes you hand-build 14 slots; this is the actual job and it should take ten seconds.

Printable season sheet with an embedded QR, the paper artifact that beats paper, because scanning it reopens the always-current version. Cheap to build, unusually sticky, and it puts our URL on 14 refrigerators.

Visible privacy posture on the shared page: kids shown as first name + last initial by default, parent phone numbers opt-in per family, and a plain-language line stating nothing is uploaded. Turns our constraint into the exact thing SignUpGenius and Stack Sports get criticized for.
A trust line on the recipient view, 'No ads. No account. Nothing tracked.', directly answering the documented 'I thought this link was spam' reflex that kills competitors' share flows.

Rain-delay / change banner: the organizer types one line and it pins to the top of the shared link with a timestamp, no message blast required. Handles the single most common real event in a youth sports season.
Season .ics download that requires no calendar permission at all, we hand over a file rather than asking for 'allow full access,' which TeamReach users explicitly resent.

Import a schedule by pasting the league's emailed text block and letting the app parse dates/opponents/fields into rows. Setup speed is where we beat the group text; typing 14 games by hand on a Sunday night is where organizers quit.

aesthetic.categoryConventions: Two visual families dominate. (1) The incumbent SaaS look, TeamSnap, SportsEngine, Stack Sports: navy-and-white, dense dashboards, five-icon tab bars, card stacks, stock photography of kids high-fiving, and an ad rail. (2) The friendly-European look, Spond, Heja: generous whitespace, rounded cards, soft shadows, one bright accent, near-illustrative icons. Family 2 is the current benchmark; family 1 is what reviewers mean when they say 'dated.' Explicitly dated markers to avoid: skeuomorphic clipboard/whistle/scoreboard iconography, italic 'sporty' display type, diagonal-stripe jersey motifs, the red/navy/white athletic cliché, gradient pill buttons, a full-season table as the landing screen, and any login wall before content. SignUpGenius is directly criticized on Capterra for looking dated, which makes visual quality an unusually cheap competitive win here. One nuance specific to us: this app sits next to real team colors, a jersey photo, a league logo, a school's red-and-gold, so the chrome must be warm and neutral enough to host someone else's colors without clashing.
aesthetic.emotionalContext: There are two distinct users in very different states, and the design must serve both without compromise. THE ORGANIZER (team parent / team mom) is at the kitchen table on a Sunday night, tired, doing part of the ~4.2 hrs/week of unpaid volunteer labor that 61% of sports parents take on, with a deadline of 'before the first game.' Their real emotion is dread of being nagged and of being the one who dropped it. What they need is the feeling of DONE, the whole season entered fast, one link out, permission to stop thinking about it. Reward that with a clear completion state, not a dashboard that implies ongoing work. THE RECIPIENT PARENT is standing in a grocery aisle on Friday night, or in the driver's seat at 7:40am Saturday with sun on the screen, one hand on the phone, a kid asking questions from the back. They are answering exactly one of three questions, is it my snack turn, what time and where, what color shirt, and they will give the page about four seconds. If the answer isn't visible at a glance they text the team parent, which is the exact failure the app exists to prevent. Design consequences: answer-first layout with the current answer in large type above any navigation; body text 17-18px minimum and the 'next up' answer at 28px+; contrast targeted at 7:1 rather than the 4.5:1 floor, because direct sunlight collapses perceived contrast on a phone at auto-brightness; tap targets at least 48px with real spacing, because fall and winter seasons mean cold hands and gloves; no hover-dependent affordances; LIGHT mode as the default (outdoors, light beats dark) with a genuine dark mode for the Sunday-night setup pass and evening games; and no confirm dialogs or multi-step flows on the parent side, which is read-only anyway.
aesthetic.recommendedFeel: Warm, communal, plainspoken, unhurried, sturdy, legible-in-sunlight. It should feel like a well-made handout from a neighbor who has their act together, not a sports SaaS dashboard, and not a cutesy family-organizer app.

colorRecommendation.hueFamily: Burnt clay / terracotta, OKLCH hue ~20-24, chroma ~0.15, on WARM (cream) paper, with a deep espresso-brown ink instead of pure black. Concretely: clay-orange primary in the #B4541F-#C9662A range, cream paper around #FBF6EF, ink around #2C221B. NOTE: this is a CHANGE from the app's current skin entry, which sits at hue 258 (cool violet, cool paper).
colorRecommendation.rationale: Two reasons, one emotional and one portfolio-structural. Emotionally, warm clay is the color of a Saturday morning field, orange slices at halftime, and the concession stand, it reads volunteer-run and communal rather than corporate, which is exactly the brand gap against navy-blue TeamSnap. It also holds up outdoors: clay on cream and cream on clay both survive glare, and because it sits off the primary-color axis it does not fight the real team colors (blue, red, green jerseys and league logos) that will appear beside it. Structurally, I read /workspaces/SWS-apps/design/skins.mjs: the 23 hues are 8, 38, 58, 72, 86, 104, 124, 142, 158, 174, 188, 202, 218, 234, 250, 258, 264, 276, 294, 310, 322, 336, 350. The single widest gap on the wheel is 8 → 38, so ~22 is the one genuinely uncontested slot in the portfolio. Team Parent currently occupies hue 258, the most crowded neighborhood in the studio, caregiver-log 250, signature-maker 264, pdf-tools 276, all within 18 degrees, and it is cool/technical, which fights the warmth this app needs. Moving it to ~22 fixes both problems at once. On the other axes I recommend paper 'warm' and voice 'editorial' while keeping texture 'band' (a clay band across the top reads as a team banner stripe, thematically apt). That combination, editorial + warm + band, is currently unused in the studio, which matters because the nearest sibling app, signup-sheets, is warm + technical + band at hue 58, and the two must not read as the same product. Accessibility caveat for the designer: clay-orange on cream does NOT pass AA at small sizes. Use clay for fills, the top band, large display numerals, and 'your turn' badges; set all body copy in the espresso ink. Reserve one cool secondary, a muted slate-teal, exclusively for 'changed since you last looked' and 'it's your turn' states so those two signals read instantly against an otherwise all-warm page.
colorRecommendation.avoid: Blue in every form, navy, royal, cornflower. It is the house color of TeamSnap, SportsEngine and Stack Sports so it reads as generic sports SaaS; it collides with actual team blues; and hues 202/218/234/250 are already spoken for in the portfolio. Avoid the red/navy/white athletic combination for the same cliché reason and because red carries the alert/error meaning we need for genuine cancellations. Avoid grass green, too literal, and it clashes with any field photography. Avoid marigold/amber specifically: hue 38 is already specials-planner and hue 8 is secret-santa, which is precisely why ~22 (between them, and further from both than either is from its other neighbors) is the right landing spot rather than a generic 'warm orange.' Finally, avoid a dark-first design; dark mode should exist but must not be the default for an app read in direct sunlight.

confidence: MEDIUM-HIGH overall, with specific caveats. HIGH confidence: TeamSnap's ad-removal IAPs and their prices, and its 4.8/59K rating (read directly off the App Store listing); SignUpGenius showing ads on the participant-facing signup page (confirmed on SignUpGenius's own help page, in their own words); TeamReach's join-by-code no-email model plus its 4.6/7K rating and app-reset/notification complaints (App Store); and the portfolio hue analysis (read directly from /workspaces/SWS-apps/design/skins.mjs, so the hue-gap claim is verified fact, not estimate). MEDIUM confidence: the Capterra complaint quotes for TeamSnap and SignUpGenius are real review text but came back through fetch-and-summarize, so wording may be lightly paraphrased, treat them as accurate in substance, not citable verbatim. LOW CONFIDENCE / EXPLICITLY UNVERIFIED: (1) The 'parents thought it was spam because of all the ads' quote is the single most useful line in this report but I sourced it from SignUpReady's blog, which is a COMPETING signup product, it is a rival's marketing copy quoting an unnamed user, and I could not find the original Reddit or forum post. The underlying mechanism is confirmed by SignUpGenius themselves, so the insight stands, but do not reproduce the quote as a citation in our own marketing. (2) I could not reach Reddit at all, the search engine returned zero Reddit results across four differently-phrased attempts and justuseapp returned HTTP 403. All complaint texture here is from Capterra, the App Store, and vendor/industry blogs, NOT from Reddit as the brief requested. (3) Exact SignUpGenius pricing tiers: their pricing page returned only navigation chrome; the ~$9/mo figure is a third-party comparison of a similar tool, not SignUpGenius's own number. (4) TeamSnap's current per-team price is a range assembled from secondary sources; I confirmed the Mar 1 2023 increase from TeamSnap's own help center but not the live 2026 price. (5) I found NO user complaints about GameChanger, its scale is documented via press releases and MLB coverage, but its weak points are my inference, not evidence. (6) My web search budget was exhausted mid-research (200/200 for the session), which cut short the planned Reddit pass and a fresh 2026 screenshot survey of category UIs; the aesthetic read is grounded in the reviews I did gather plus category knowledge rather than a visual audit.
